title: British far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US, DHS says | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

British right-wing provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos was deported Friday to the United Kingdom, according to a spokesperson with the Department of Homeland Security.

Yiannopoulos was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement Thursday at a Louisiana airport after overstaying his visa, DHS said.

The conservative figure was being held by ICE in Louisiana, where several ICE facilities have served as the final stop for thousands of migrants in President Donald Trump’s deportation push.

Here’s what you need to know about Yiannopoulos’ deportation,arrest and his controversial path through the far-right orbit and conservative politics.

Born in England to British and Greek parents, Yiannopoulos came to the US, where he built a career as a conservative firebrand who leaned into controversy through his writing for the far-right website Breitbart News, speeches and online presence.

He was an outspoken supporter of Donald Trump during his presidential campaign in 2016 and gained fans who appreciated his complete abandonment of political correctness.

Many of his views drew outrage from many who argued the racist and hateful language was an attempt to stoke tensions on campus and should not be platformed by colleges and universities. He has equated feminism with cancer, said America “has a Muslim problem,” disparaged transgender people andstarted a scholarshipexclusively for young, White men. He has embraced the outcry that often erupts from his comments, reportedlyproclaiming himselfthe “most fabulous supervillain on the internet.”

While he previously said he was gay – and featured his sexuality as a significant part of his gadfly brand – he has recently said he no longer identifies as such.

Yiannopoulos entered the US legally on May 14, 2019, but “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” the DHS said in a statement announcing his arrest on X.

A judge issued a final order of removal for Yiannopoulos on July 22, after he failed to appear at an immigration hearing, the agency said.

Yiannopoulos was arrested by ICE on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Kenner, Louisiana.

He was deported “back to his home country” Friday, DHS told CNN.

Border Czar Tom Homan said Sunday the speedy deportation of Yiannopoulos was part of an effort to increase the efficiency of removal proceedings, and not the result of preferential treatment of someone whose views have aligned with Trump’s.

“We’ve been working steadily the last few months on getting people out quicker,” Homan said during an interview on CNN’s “State of the Union” program. “ICE, along with CBP and the Department of Homeland Security, is working really good on the efficiencies of the removal process. Get them out quick. Open those beds up for more detainees.”

When asked whether the Trump administration wanted to make an example out of Yiannopoulos’ arrest, Homan said, “We don’t deport people based on political affiliation. As soon as we get an order of removal, our goal is removing as quick as possible, regardless of who they are.”

After his arrest, far-right influencer and Trump ally Laura Loomer – who has bitterly feuded with Yiannopoulos – wrote in apost on XFriday that she had reported him to ICE and the FBI.

“There’s a lot of people calling ICE,” Homan said Sunday. “She says she’s one. She probably was, but bottom line is, it doesn’t matter. He was ordered to be removed by an immigration judge and ICE’s job is to execute that order.”

There’s no indication that any report from Loomer had a connection to his arrest, which came at a time when ICE arrests have been happeningmore frequentlyat US airports.

It is unclear how Yiannopoulos had been operating in the US prior to 2019, as he had been employed and appeared regularly at public speaking events across the country since at least 2015. In 2017, he said he was in the US on anO-1 visafor immigrants of “extraordinary ability.” CNN has reached out to DHS for further details.

CNN is working to determine if Yiannopoulos has legal representation.

Yiannopoulos became more well-known while the conservative landscape was undergoing a tidal change, as then-presidential candidate Trump was rallying a furiously antiestablishment base, and alt-right ideas were inching closer to the mainstream.

Until 2017, he honed his voice as an outspoken senior editor at Breitbart News, where he wrote columns and gave speeches titled things like “10 Things Milo Hates About Islam” and “Sorry, Girls! But The Smartest People In The World Are All Men.”

He made it his mission to take on what he viewed as traditionally left-leaning college establishments that year, embarking on a“Dangerous F*ggot” bus tourof US universities and college campuses – in the name of promoting free speech and undermined voices – during which he argued rape culture on campuses didn’t exist, compared social justice to a disease and at times mocked individual students.

He was typically invited to speak by conservative student organizations.

Yiannopoulos’ acerbic and at times hateful speech attracted the fury of students who argued his views should not be platformed. Several of his campus events were met with protests, including one at the University of California, Berkeley that was canceled after demonstrationsbecame violent.

He positioned himself as one of Trump’s passionate supporters, sometimes jokingly referring to the president as “Daddy.” The conservative at times connected the wave of support he had received with the same conservative movement that paved Trump’s path to the presidency.

“People are tired of being told how to live, how to speak, what language they can use,” Yiannopoulos told CNN in 2017. “The strength of feeling in my crowds, the enthusiasm for me from the audiences is the same – the same instinct, the same sort of motivating force (that) put Trump in the White House.”

When asked for comment about Yiannopoulos’ arrest, the White House referred CNN to DHS.

Yiannopoulos came under intense scrutiny in February 2017 after he made comments appearing to condone pedophilia.

Yiannopoulos resigned from Breitbart amid the backlash and offered a rare apology but said the media distorted his comments. In the span of a day, he lost his book deal with publishing giant Simon & Schuster and he was disinvited from speaking at the powerful Conservative Political Action Conference.

Following the backlash, Yiannopoulos focused largely on renouncing his sexual orientation as a gay man. His Telegram account, which hasn’t seen new posts in more than a year, said he was opening a clinic in Florida that would help “men plagued by same-sex attraction.”He also told Tucker Carlsonlast year, “mainstreaming homosexuality in the Republican Party is the great regret of my life.”

Twitter banned Yiannopoulos in 2016. His Facebookaccount was also taken downin 2019, further limiting his online presence.

In a 2022 Telegram post, he said he was an unpaid intern to former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, a lightning-rod Republican from Georgia.

Yiannopoulos also continued to have his eye on national politics, working on the 2024 presidential campaign of Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, who fell from grace afterpraising Adolf Hitler andmaking aseries of antisemitic comments.

Ye performed atCaesars Superdomein New Orleans Friday, the same day Yiannopoulos was deported.

After Elon Musk bought Twitter, now known as X, Yiannopoulos had his account reinstated and remained prolific online. Yiannopoulos posted on X as recently as Thursday, the day federal officials detained him in Louisiana.

Yiannopoulos has frequently called for aggressive immigration enforcement in posts on his X account over the last year.

After Trump returned to the White House on a campaign to dramatically increase deportations of undocumented people, Yiannopoulos insisted the administration needed to make good on that promise.

“There is one concrete thing we must insist on this administration delivering,” Yiannopoulos said in aJune 2025 X post.“It matters a lot more than debts measured in imaginary money. We have got to deport millions and millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters.”

In September 2025, nearly two weeks after aMexican man was fatally shotby ICE in Minneapolis, Yiannopouloscalled for“total legal immunity for ICE agents when they’re on duty.”

He had alsocalled forICE checkpoints in heavily trafficked areas in California, like gas stations and intersections, and “on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally.”
